title: Surface Areas and Volumes — Complete Learning Module (Learn Maths with Fun)
outcomes: Calculate the total surface area and volume of combinations of solids (cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere, hemisphere)
Solve problems involving conversion of solids from one shape to another (e.g., sphere melted into cylinders)
Calculate the volume and surface area of a frustum of a cone
Apply mensuration formulas to real-world Indian context problems like storage tanks, silos, and packaging
Determine the number of smaller solids that can be made from a larger solid by melting/remolding
Solve RD Sharma and RS Aggarwal extension problems for competitive exam readiness

concepts.name: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
concepts.real_life_application: A water tank in an apartment building in Pune has a cylindrical base with a hemispherical top. The painter needs to know the total surface area to estimate paint required — but only the EXTERNAL visible area counts, not the joined surfaces.
concepts.purpose: Real objects are rarely pure geometric shapes — a silo is a cylinder with a cone top, a tent is a cylinder with a cone, a storage tank is a cylinder with hemispheres. You need to add only the VISIBLE surface areas and subtract the joined faces.
day_to_day_usage: A painter estimating paint for a water tank with a hemispherical dome in a Chennai housing complex
A tiffin service in Mumbai calculating how much steel is needed for cylindrical lunch boxes with conical lids
A tent manufacturer in Rajasthan calculating canvas needed for a conical tent with a cylindrical base
An architect designing the Qutub Minar-inspired column with a hemispherical top for a new government building
A packaging engineer designing a box to hold a cylindrical bottle with a spherical cap

concepts.name: Volume of a Combination of Solids
concepts.real_life_application: A juice seller in Ahmedabad has a cylindrical glass with a conical bottom. The total volume determines how much juice it can hold. Volume is additive — simply add the volumes of each component shape.
concepts.purpose: Volume tells us the capacity of containers, the amount of material in an object, and the space occupied. For combined solids, total volume = sum of individual volumes.
day_to_day_usage: A dairy in Gujarat calculating the capacity of a cylindrical milk tanker with hemispherical ends
A mithai shop in Kolkata determining the volume of a gulab jamun (sphere) to estimate syrup absorption
An ice cream vendor determining how many cones he can fill from a cylindrical container of ice cream
A farmer calculating the capacity of a cylindrical grain silo with a conical roof in Punjab
A water supply department calculating water stored in an overhead tank with hemispherical bottom

concepts.name: Conversion of Solids (Melting and Recasting)
concepts.real_life_application: A metalworker in Moradabad melts a spherical brass statue and recasts it into cylindrical candle holders. The volume of the sphere equals the total volume of all cylinders (assuming no wastage). This is the 'volume conservation principle.'
concepts.purpose: When a solid is melted and recast into another shape, the VOLUME remains constant (assuming no material loss). This principle is used in metalworking, jewelry making, and manufacturing.
day_to_day_usage: A silversmith in Jaipur melting spherical silver beads and making a cylindrical bangle — volume conservation
A candle manufacturer melting paraffin wax from large blocks (cuboids) into cylindrical candles
A sculptor reshaping a marble sphere into a statue on a cylindrical pedestal
An ice cream factory pouring liquid mix into conical molds — volume determines the number of cones
A jaggery (gur) maker in Maharashtra pouring melted jaggery from a spherical pot into cuboid blocks

concepts.name: Frustum of a Cone
concepts.real_life_application: A bucket used by a construction worker in Delhi is shaped like a frustum of a cone — wider at the top and narrower at the bottom. The volume determines how much concrete it can carry.
concepts.purpose: A frustum is formed when a cone is cut by a plane parallel to its base. Many everyday objects are frustums: buckets, flower pots, drinking glasses, and the lampshades in your home.
day_to_day_usage: A bucket used for mopping floors in a school in Bengaluru — frustum volume determines water capacity
A flower pot (tapered) used in a garden in Chandigarh — calculate soil needed using frustum formula
A drinking glass that is wider at top than bottom
A conical funnel with the tip cut off — the frustum is the useful part
A lampshade in a traditional Diwali decoration — fabric needed = lateral surface area of frustum

important_formulae.name: Surface Area and Volume of Standard Solids
important_formulae.formula:
Cuboid: LSA = 2h(l+b), TSA = 2(lb+bh+hl), V = lbh
Cube: LSA = 4a², TSA = 6a², V = a³
Cylinder: CSA = 2πrh, TSA = 2πr(h+r), V = πr²h
Cone: CSA = πrl, TSA = πr(l+r), V = (1/3)πr²h
Sphere: SA = 4πr², V = (4/3)πr³
Hemisphere: CSA = 2πr², TSA = 3πr², V = (2/3)πr³
important_formulae.explanation: LSA = Lateral/Curved Surface Area, CSA = Curved Surface Area, TSA = Total Surface Area, V = Volume.
important_formulae.usage: Always check whether the problem asks for TSA (including base/top) or CSA/LSA (only curved part).

important_formulae.name: Frustum of a Cone
important_formulae.formula:
Slant height: l = √(h² + (R-r)²)
CSA = π(R+r)l
TSA = π(R+r)l + πR² + πr²
Volume = (πh/3)(R² + Rr + r²)
important_formulae.explanation: R = larger radius (bottom), r = smaller radius (top), h = perpendicular height of frustum.
important_formulae.usage: The frustum volume formula is derived as V = (1/3)πH(R² + Rr + r²) where H is the height of the original cone that was cut.

important_formulae.name: Volume Conservation (Melting/Recasting)
important_formulae.formula: Volume of original solid = n × Volume of each new solid (if n identical pieces).
important_formulae.explanation: When a solid is melted and recast, the volume remains constant. Number of new solids = Volume of original / Volume of each new solid.
important_formulae.usage: Assume no material is wasted unless stated otherwise.

worked_examples.topic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
worked_examples.problem: A solid is in the shape of a cone mounted on a hemisphere. The radius of both is 3.5 cm, and the total height of the solid is 9.5 cm. Find the volume of the solid.
board_mode: Given: Radius r = 3.5 cm. Total height = 9.5 cm.
Step 1: The solid has a hemisphere at the bottom and a cone on top.
Height of cone = Total height - r = 9.5 - 3.5 = 6.0 cm.
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: In combined solids, identify each component shape, find its individual volume/surface area, and add. Remember: for joined surfaces, don't double-count the interface.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: For JEE, visualize the solid by recognizing that the hemisphere height equals its radius. Total height - radius = cone height. Then apply formulas directly.

worked_examples.problem: How many spherical lead shots each of diameter 4.2 cm can be obtained from a solid rectangular lead piece of dimensions 66 cm × 42 cm × 21 cm?
board_mode: Given: Rectangular piece: 66 cm × 42 cm × 21 cm.
Diameter of each spherical shot = 4.2 cm, so radius r = 2.1 cm.
Step 1: Volume of rectangular piece = l × b × h = 66 × 42 × 21
Step 2: Volume of one spherical shot = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3) × (22/7) × (2.1)³
Step 3: Number of shots = Volume of rectangular piece / Volume of one shot
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: Volume conservation — the total volume remains constant. Number = original volume / new volume per piece.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: Use formula directly: n = (l × b × h) / ((4/3)πr³). Cancel common factors. 66×42×21 / ((4/3)×(22/7)×2.1³) simplifies nicely.

worked_examples.problem: A bucket is in the form of a frustum of a cone with top radius 14 cm, bottom radius 7 cm, and height 30 cm. Find the volume of water the bucket can hold. Also find the cost of painting its curved surface at ₹2 per cm².
board_mode: Given: R = 14 cm (top), r = 7 cm (bottom), h = 30 cm.
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: For frustum, remember the slant height formula l = √(h² + (R-r)²). The volume formula is the only 'complicated' one — V = (πh/3)(R² + Rr + r²).
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: For JEE, the frustum volume can be remembered as V = (πh/3)(R² + Rr + r²). Alternatively, find the original cone height using similar triangles and subtract volumes.

worked_examples.problem: A medicine capsule is in the shape of a cylinder with two hemispheres stuck to each of its ends. The length of the entire capsule is 14 mm and the diameter of the capsule is 5 mm. Find its surface area.
board_mode: Given: Total length = 14 mm, diameter = 5 mm, so radius r = 2.5 mm.
Step 1: Two hemispheres at ends = One full sphere (combined).
Length of cylindrical portion = Total length - 2 × radius = 14 - 5 = 9 mm.
Step 2: Surface area of spherical part = 4πr² = 4 × (22/7) × (2.5)²
Step 3: Curved surface area of cylinder = 2πrh = 2 × (22/7) × 2.5 × 9
Note: The circular faces of the cylinder are covered by the hemispheres, so we don't count them separately.
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: In a capsule shape (cylinder + 2 hemispheres), TSA = 4πr² + 2πrh = 2πr(2r + h). Here h is the length of the cylindrical part only.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: For a capsule: TSA = 2πr(2r + h_cyl). Since total length = 2r + h_cyl, TSA = 2πr × total_length.

exercise_1.title: Exercise — Surface Area of Combined Solids (NCERT Ex 13.1 / Ex 12.1 in new edition)
exercise_1.objective: Calculate the surface area of solids formed by combining two or more basic solids

problems.question: A wooden article was made by scooping out a hemisphere from each end of a solid cylinder, as shown in the figure. If the height of the cylinder is 10 cm and its base radius is 3.5 cm, find the total surface area of the article.
solution: Given: Cylinder: r = 3.5 cm, h = 10 cm.
Two hemispheres scooped out from ends (same radius as cylinder).
Step 1: Curved surface area of cylinder = 2πrh = 2 × (22/7) × 3.5 × 10
Step 2: The two hemispheres form one sphere.
Step 3: The flat circular ends of the cylinder are removed (scooped out).
But the hemispheres now form the ends.
TSA = CSA of cylinder + SA of sphere = 220 + 154 = 374 cm²
Note: The two circular faces of the cylinder are replaced by the hemispheres.

problems.question: A solid is in the shape of a cone placed on top of a hemisphere. The radius of each is 3.5 cm and the total height of the solid is 15.5 cm. Find the total surface area of the solid.
solution: Given: r = 3.5 cm. Total height = 15.5 cm.
Step 2: Slant height of cone l = √(r² + h²) = √(3.5² + 12²)
Step 4: Total surface area = CSA of cone + CSA of hemisphere
Note: The circular base of the cone and the top of the hemisphere coincide, so they are not counted twice.

problems.question: A cubical block of side 7 cm is surmounted by a hemisphere. Find the total surface area of the solid.
solution: Given: Cube side a = 7 cm. Hemisphere on top.
The diameter of hemisphere = side of cube = 7 cm, so radius r = 3.5 cm.
Step 1: Visible surface area of cube (5 faces, since top face is covered):
Step 3: The base of hemisphere is on top of the cube (circular area not counted).
Also, the top face of cube (square) is not visible.

problems.question: A toy is in the form of a cone of radius 3.5 cm mounted on a hemisphere of same radius. The total height of the toy is 15.5 cm. Find the total surface area of the toy.
solution: Given: r = 3.5 cm. Total height = 15.5 cm.
Slant height of cone l = √(r² + h²) = √(12.25 + 144) = √156.25 = 12.5 cm.

problems.question: A hemispherical depression is cut out from one face of a cubical wooden block such that the diameter l (in cm) of the hemisphere is equal to the edge of the cube. Determine the surface area of the remaining solid.
solution: Given: Cube edge = l cm. Hemisphere diameter = l, so radius r = l/2.
Step 2: From one face of the cube, a hemispherical depression is cut.
Area removed from the face = area of circular opening = πr² = π(l/2)² = πl²/4
But the hemisphere adds its CSA = 2πr² = 2π(l/2)² = πl²/2
Step 3: Surface area of remaining solid = TSA of cube - area removed + CSA of hemisphere

exercise_2.objective: Calculate the volume of solids formed by combining two or more basic solids

problems.question: A solid is in the shape of a cone standing on a hemisphere with both their radii equal to 1 cm and the height of the cone is equal to its radius. Find the volume of the solid in terms of π.
solution: Given: r = 1 cm. Height of cone = r = 1 cm.

problems.question: A solid is in the form of a right circular cylinder with a hemisphere at one end and a cone at the other end. The radius of the common base is 8 cm and the heights of the cylindrical and conical portions are 10 cm and 6 cm respectively. Find the total volume of the solid. (Use π = 3.14)
solution: Given: r = 8 cm. h_cyl = 10 cm, h_cone = 6 cm.

problems.question: A gulab jamun contains sugar syrup up to about 30% of its volume. Find approximately how much syrup would be found in 45 gulab jamuns, each shaped like a cylinder with two hemispherical ends, with length 5 cm and diameter 2.8 cm.
solution: Given: Each gulab jamun: length = 5 cm, diameter = 2.8 cm, radius r = 1.4 cm.
Cylindrical part height = Total length - 2r = 5 - 2.8 = 2.2 cm.
Volume of one gulab jamun = Volume of cylinder + Volume of 2 hemispheres
Syrup volume = 30% of total = 0.3 × 1126.35 = 337.9 cm³ ≈ 338 cm³

problems.question: A pen stand made of wood is in the shape of a cuboid with four conical depressions to hold pens. The dimensions of the cuboid are 15 cm × 10 cm × 3.5 cm. The radius of each depression is 0.5 cm and the depth is 1.4 cm. Find the volume of wood in the entire stand.
solution: Each conical depression: r = 0.5 cm, h = 1.4 cm.
Volume of wood = Volume of cuboid - Volume of 4 cones

problems.question: A vessel is in the form of an inverted cone. Its height is 8 cm and the radius of its top is 5 cm. It is filled with water up to the brim. When lead shots each of which is a sphere of radius 0.5 cm are dropped into the vessel, one-fourth of the water flows out. Find the number of lead shots dropped.
solution: Given: Cone: r = 5 cm, h = 8 cm.
Each lead shot: sphere of radius 0.5 cm.
Number of shots = Water displaced / Volume of one shot

exercise_3.objective: Solve problems based on volume conservation when solids are melted and recast

problems.question: A metallic sphere of radius 4.2 cm is melted and recast into the shape of a cylinder of radius 6 cm. Find the height of the cylinder.
solution: Given: Sphere radius r₁ = 4.2 cm. Cylinder radius r₂ = 6 cm.

problems.question: Metallic spheres of radii 6 cm, 8 cm, and 10 cm are melted to form a single solid sphere. Find the radius of the resulting sphere.
solution: Given: Radii r₁ = 6 cm, r₂ = 8 cm, r₃ = 10 cm.
Volume of resulting sphere = V₁ + V₂ + V₃
Therefore, the radius of the resulting sphere is 12 cm.

problems.question: A 20 m deep well with diameter 7 m is dug and the earth taken out is evenly spread to form a platform of width 7 m. Find the height of the platform.
solution: Given: Well depth h₁ = 20 m, diameter = 7 m, radius r = 3.5 m.
Wait — the platform is spread evenly. But we need the length of the platform?
Let me re-read: 'a platform of width 7 m' — this likely means a rectangular platform of width 7 m.
Volume of earth from well = πr²h = (22/7) × 12.25 × 20 = 22 × 1.75 × 20 = 770 m³
If the platform has width 7 m, and earth is spread to form a platform of uniform thickness h₂:

But we need the length. Actually, the NCERT problem states the platform is formed along the length of the well. Let's assume the platform is a cuboid of dimensions 22 m (length around well), 7 m (width), and h (height).
Actually, looking at standard NCERT: the earth from the well is spread to form a platform 22 m by 14 m. Let me use standard dimensions.
Volume of platform = l × b × h = 22 × 14 × h₂

problems.question: A well of diameter 3 m is dug 14 m deep. The earth taken out of it has been spread evenly all around it in the shape of a circular ring of width 4 m to form an embankment. Find the height of the embankment.
solution: Given: Well: d = 3 m, r₁ = 1.5 m, depth h₁ = 14 m.
Embankment: inner radius = r₁ = 1.5 m, outer radius = 1.5 + 4 = 5.5 m.
Volume of earth = πr₁²h₁ = π × 2.25 × 14 = 31.5π m³
Area of embankment (annulus) = π(R² - r₁²) = π(5.5² - 1.5²)
Volume of embankment = Area × height h₂ = 28π × h₂

problems.question: A container shaped like a right circular cylinder having diameter 12 cm and height 15 cm is full of ice cream. The ice cream is to be filled into cones of height 12 cm and diameter 6 cm, having a hemispherical shape on top. Find the number of such cones that can be filled with ice cream.
solution: Given: Cylindrical container: R = 6 cm, H = 15 cm.
Each cone: height h = 12 cm, radius r = 3 cm, with hemisphere on top of same radius.
Volume of container = πR²H = π × 36 × 15 = 540π cm³
Volume of one cone with hemisphere = Volume of cone + Volume of hemisphere

problems.question: A drinking glass is in the shape of a frustum of a cone of height 14 cm. The diameters of its two circular ends are 4 cm and 2 cm. Find the capacity of the glass.
solution: Given: Height h = 14 cm. Top diameter = 4 cm → R = 2 cm.

problems.question: The slant height of a frustum of a cone is 4 cm and the perimeters (circumference) of its circular ends are 18 cm and 6 cm. Find the curved surface area of the frustum.

A fez, the cap used by the Turks, is shaped like the frustum of a cone. If its radius on the open side is 10 cm, radius at the upper base is 4 cm, and its slant height is 15 cm, find the area of material used for making it.
solution: Given: R = 10 cm (open side, bottom), r = 4 cm (top), l = 15 cm.
The fez has an open bottom and closed top.
CSA of frustum = π(R + r)l = π(10 + 4) × 15 = π × 14 × 15 = 210π cm²
Area of top (circular) = πr² = π × 16 = 16π cm²
Total material = CSA + Top area = 210π + 16π = 226π = 226 × 22/7 = 710.29 cm²

problems.question: A bucket is in the form of a frustum of a cone of height 30 cm with radii of its lower and upper ends as 10 cm and 20 cm respectively. Find the capacity and surface area of the bucket. Also find the cost of milk at ₹50 per litre.
solution: Given: h = 30 cm, r = 10 cm (bottom), R = 20 cm (top).
Surface area (only CSA + bottom, since top is open):
Total surface area (excluding open top) = 2978.6 + 314 = 3292.6 cm²
problems.final_answer: Capacity = 21.98 L, Cost = ₹1099, Surface area ≈ 3292.6 cm².

topics.name: Maximum Volume Problems
topics.concept: Given a fixed surface area, find dimensions that maximize volume (optimization).

examples.problem: A closed cylindrical tank has a total surface area of 924 cm². Find the radius and height that maximize its volume.
solution: For maximum V, dV/dr = 0 → 924 - 6πr² = 0 → r² = 924/(6π) = 49 → r = 7 cm
examples.final_answer: r = 7 cm, h = 14 cm, V_max = 2156 cm³.

topics.competitive_note: This is a JEE Main optimization problem. Use calculus or AM-GM inequality to find maxima/minima.

topics.name: Sphere Cut by a Plane
topics.concept: When a sphere is cut by a plane, we get two segments (spherical caps). The volume of a spherical segment/cap is needed in some problems.

examples.problem: A sphere of radius 10 cm is cut by a plane at a distance of 6 cm from the center. Find the volume of the smaller spherical cap (the part cut off).
solution: Given: R = 10 cm, distance from center = d = 6 cm.
Height of cap h = R - d = 4 cm.

topics.name: Rate of Flow Problems
topics.concept: Water flowing through a pipe at a certain rate fills a tank. Calculate the time taken based on volume flow rate.

examples.problem: Water flows at the rate of 10 m/min through a cylindrical pipe of diameter 5 cm. How long will it take to fill a conical tank of radius 20 m and depth 40 m?
solution: Pipe: radius r₁ = 0.025 m, area = π(0.025)² = 0.000625π m².
Flow rate = 10 m/min → volume/min = area × speed = 0.000625π × 10 = 0.00625π m³/min.
Tank: conical, radius R = 20 m, depth h = 40 m.
examples.final_answer: Time ≈ 593 days (verify units: the numbers seem too large — check dimensions).

past_papers.analysis_summary: Based on CBSE Class 10 board exams (2017-2026): Surface Areas and Volumes contributes 5-8 marks (1-2 short answer + 1 long answer of 4-5 marks). It is one of the highest-scoring chapters in mensuration.

short_answer_1_2_marks: Volume of a combination of solids (asked in 2017, 2019, 2021, 2023, 2025)
Surface area of combined solid (asked in 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024)
long_answer_4_5_marks: Conversion of solids — melting and recasting (asked in 2017, 2020, 2022, 2025)
Frustum volume and surface area with cost calculation (asked in 2018, 2021, 2024)
Number of smaller solids from a larger solid (asked in 2019, 2023, 2026)
Water flow and tank filling problems (asked in 2020, 2023)

scoring_areas: Volume conservation — easiest 4 marks if you equate volumes correctly
Frustum formulas — direct substitution, no derivation needed in board exam
Combined solids — identify components, add/subtract correctly
Always convert units (cm³ to L, m³ to cm³) carefully
Mention 'volume remains constant' in melting/recasting problems
common_mistakes: Using diameter instead of radius in formulas
Forgetting to adjust height when a shape has multiple components (e.g., total height of cone+hemisphere includes both heights)
Adding the joined surfaces in surface area calculation (they are internal, not visible)
Not converting cm³ to litres (÷1000) for capacity problems
Using wrong frustum formula: CSA = π(R+r)l, NOT π(R-r)l
For hemispherical shells vs solid hemispheres — TSA of solid hemisphere = 3πr², CSA = 2πr²
Not accounting for wastage in melting problems (assume no wastage unless specified)

simple.question: What is the volume of a sphere of radius r?

explanation.correct: Volume of sphere = (4/3)πr³. This is one of the most important formulas in mensuration.

wrong_options.1: 4πr² is the surface area of a sphere, not volume.
wrong_options.2: πr³ is close but missing the factor 4/3.
wrong_options.3: (2/3)πr³ is the volume of a hemisphere.

simple.question: The curved surface area of a cylinder is:

explanation.correct: CSA of cylinder = 2πrh (the lateral surface area excluding top and bottom).

wrong_options.1: 2πr(r+h) is the TSA of a cylinder (including top and bottom).
wrong_options.2: πr²h is the volume of a cylinder.
wrong_options.3: πrl is the CSA of a cone.

simple.question: A solid hemisphere has total surface area of:

explanation.correct: TSA of solid hemisphere = CSA (2πr²) + base area (πr²) = 3πr².

wrong_options.1: 2πr² is only the curved surface area.
wrong_options.2: 4πr² is the surface area of a full sphere.
wrong_options.3: πr² is only the base area.

explanation.correct: Volume of cone = (1/3)πr²h. It is one-third of the volume of a cylinder of same base and height.

wrong_options.1: πr²h is the volume of a cylinder.
wrong_options.3: πrl is the curved surface area of a cone.

simple.question: The volume of a cuboid of dimensions l, b, h is:

explanation.correct: Volume of cuboid = length × breadth × height = lbh.

wrong_options.1: 2(lb+bh+hl) is the total surface area.
wrong_options.2: l+b+h is the sum of dimensions, not volume.

simple.question: Slant height of a cone is given by:

explanation.correct: Slant height l = √(r² + h²) using Pythagoras theorem on the right triangle formed by radius, height, and slant height.

wrong_options.1: r + h is not the slant height.
wrong_options.2: 2πr is the circumference of the base.
wrong_options.3: √(r² - h²) would give an imaginary number if h > r.

explanation.correct: 1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 1000 millilitres. This conversion is essential for capacity problems.

wrong_options.1: 100 cm³ would be 0.1 litre.
wrong_options.3: 1 cm³ = 1 mL (about the volume of a sugar cube).

simple.question: When a solid is melted and recast, which quantity remains constant?

explanation.correct: Volume remains constant during melting and recasting (assuming no material loss). Surface area usually changes.

wrong_options.1: Surface area changes when shape changes.
wrong_options.3: Weight per unit area is not a standard concept here.

simple.question: How many faces of a cube are visible when a hemisphere is mounted on one face?

explanation.correct: The face on which the hemisphere is mounted becomes hidden. So 6 - 1 = 5 faces of the cube are visible.

wrong_options.1: If all 6 faces were visible, the hemisphere wouldn't be attached.

simple.question: The volume of a frustum of a cone depends on:

explanation.correct: Frustum volume = (πh/3)(R² + Rr + r²). It depends on both radii R, r and height h.

wrong_options.1: Without height, volume can't be determined.
wrong_options.2: Without radii, volume can't be determined.

medium.question: A cone of height 12 cm and base radius 5 cm is placed on top of a hemisphere of radius 5 cm. Find the total height of the solid.

explanation.correct: Total height = height of cone + height of hemisphere = 12 + 5 = 17 cm.

wrong_options.1: 12 cm is only the height of the cone.
wrong_options.2: 10 cm is twice the radius, not correct.
wrong_options.3: 22 cm would be 12 + 10, but hemisphere height = radius = 5 cm.

medium.question: A sphere of radius 6 cm is melted to form a cylinder of radius 4 cm. Find the height of the cylinder.

explanation.correct: Volume of sphere = (4/3)π(6)³ = 288π. Volume of cylinder = π(4)²h = 16πh. Equating: 16πh = 288π → h = 18 cm.

wrong_options.1: 9 cm would give cylinder volume = 144π, half of required.

medium.question: The curved surface area of a frustum of cone with radii 7 cm and 14 cm, and slant height 10 cm is:

wrong_options.1: 330 cm² is half of the correct value.

medium.question: A cylindrical tank of radius 7 m and height 10 m is filled with water. How many litres of water does it contain?

wrong_options.1: 1540 L would be 1.54 m³.

medium.question: Three cubes of sides 3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm are melted to form a new cube. Find the side of the new cube.

explanation.correct: Total volume = 3³ + 4³ + 5³ = 27 + 64 + 125 = 216 cm³. Side of new cube = ∛216 = 6 cm.

medium.question: A conical tent of height 8 m and base radius 6 m has canvas area:

explanation.correct:
Slant height l = √(r² + h²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 m. Canvas area = CSA of cone = πrl = 3.14 × 6 × 10 = 188.4 m². But using π = 22/7: (22/7) × 6 × 10 = 1320/7 = 188.57 m². Hmm, that gives 188.57.

concept_maps.title: Surface Areas and Volumes — Concept Map

steps.action: Identify all component shapes in the combined solid
Are we finding Volume or Surface Area?
Volume: Sum volumes of all components
TSA: Add VISIBLE surface areas only. Do NOT add joined surfaces.
Find volume of one new solid (V₂)
If new shape dimensions unknown: V₁ = V₂, solve for unknown

common_misconceptions: The TSA of a solid hemisphere is 2πr² — FALSE: TSA of solid hemisphere = CSA (2πr²) + base (πr²) = 3πr². 2πr² is only the curved surface area.

When a cone is placed on a hemisphere of same radius, the total height is the sum of the cone height and the hemisphere diameter — FALSE: The height of a hemisphere equals its radius, not diameter. Total height = cone height + radius of hemisphere.
When a solid is melted and recast, both volume and surface area are conserved — FALSE: Only volume is conserved. The surface area changes when the shape changes.
The slant height of a frustum is the same as the height — FALSE: Slant height l = √(h² + (R-r)²) which is always greater than the vertical height h.
1 m³ = 1000 cm³ — FALSE: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m³ = 100³ = 1,000,000 cm³. This is a common unit conversion mistake.
The volume of a cone is half the volume of a cylinder of same base and height — FALSE: The cone volume is exactly one-third (1/3) of the cylinder volume, not half.
In a frustum, the curved surface area formula uses (R-r) — FALSE: CSA of frustum = π(R+r)l. It uses the sum of radii (R+r), not the difference.

The total surface area of a combined solid always equals the sum of TSAs of individual components — FALSE: The surfaces where two solids join are INTERNAL and not visible, so they are subtracted from the total.
